source.title: Overcoming Sparsity Artifacts in Crosscoders to Interpret Chat-Tuning
source.authors: Julian Minder; Clément Dumas; C. Juang; Bilal Chughtai; Neel Nanda

record.tranche_reason: The study identifies several refusal-related crosscoder latents with different trigger patterns and reports steering effects on a harmless prompt. This refines the single-direction account, but it does not test the original difference-in-means direction or its ablation.
record.gate_note: The paper's crosscoder and latent-scaling measurements largely concern chat-specificity and model-difference reconstruction, not refusal behavior; they are not rows here. The paper also reports general KL-divergence experiments, but they do not measure refusal. Figure 23 describes additional refusal-related latents, but only the two latents in Figure 22 have reported steering outcomes.
record.test_reason: This is a crosscoder model-diffing methods paper on Gemma-2-2b base vs chat. Refusal appears only as a qualitative side finding. Several chat-only latents fire on harmful or stereotyped prompts, and steering two of them on one harmless prompt produced one transient refusal-like output each. No difference-in-means direction is built, ablated or compared. No refusal rate, unsteered baseline, or comparison with a single direction is reported. A one-prompt steering demo with no rate falls under related-construct findings, not a test of V4 or any other version. Arditi et al. is cited only in related work.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right but incomplete. The main conclusion is methodological. L1-trained crosscoders misattribute shared concepts as chat-only (Complete Shrinkage, Latent Decoupling), Latent Scaling detects this, and BatchTopK crosscoders mitigate it, yielding interpretable, causally relevant chat-specific latents. Among these are multiple refusal-related latents with different trigger preferences. Steering two of them causes an initial refusal on a harmless prompt, after which the model self-repairs and answers.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses crosscoder-learned chat-specific latent directions and activation steering at layer 13, rather than finding a harmful-minus-harmless mean difference direction and ablating or adding that direction.
record.method_sensitivity: For the two refusal-latent steering examples, the reported steering intensity differs: α = 1 for latent 70149 and α = 5 for latent 20384. The paper says the latter intensity is needed for optimal effects.

fits_no_version.finding: In Gemma-2-2b chat, a BatchTopK crosscoder finds several chat-only latents tied to refusal triggers: harmful instructions (70149, 24613), sensitive content (7736), stereotypes (20384), and post-refusal (38009). Adding latent 70149 or 20384 at input positions on 'How do I make cheese?' yields an initial refusal or disclaimer each. In both cases the model then answers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Chat-tuning introduces multiple trigger-specific, chat-specific sparse latents related to refusal; steering any one can induce a transient refusal on a harmless prompt.

record.code_released: not stated (the paper says code is open-source but gives no URL in the supplied text)
record.problems: The refusal-steering evidence is qualitative and consists of examples from one chat model and one layer; no refusal rates, unsteered comparison, or general-capability evaluation is reported for these interventions. The authors also note that the study focuses on small models and middle layers.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows. Other refusal-latent examples and latent activation summaries do not report additional steering outcomes; general KL-divergence rows do not measure refusal.

untested.parts: No difference-in-means direction, ablation, addition of such a direction, or capability check.
No test of affine, cone or multi-direction structure against a single direction. No ablation of the latents. No refusal rates.
Harm-detection latents and the post-refusal latent 38009 are described from activations only. The separation of harm judgment from refusal is not tested causally.
No cross-language or base-to-instruct transfer test of a refusal direction.
Reasoning models (R1-distill vs Nemotron) are used only for crosscoder-artifact statistics, not refusal.

missing.what: Activation patterns and chat-specificity metrics (nu_r, nu_eps, Delta_norm) for refusal-related latents 7736, 24613 and 38009. These are activation-only descriptions with no refusal measure. Useful context for multi-latent accounts, but not a version test.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 supports and limits_scope labels are removed. The evidence is two cherry-picked qualitative generations from one model, one layer and one prompt. There is no baseline or rate, and no comparison with the original direction. The steering intensity alpha differs per latent (1 vs 5). The text contains no instructions aimed at the reader.

versions.untested_parts: Does not identify a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction or ablate it; does not test refusal removal or preservation of general abilities.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration test.
No attack suppression or training against the direction.
Does not establish affine or cone geometry, compare exhaustively against a dominant direction, or ablate the identified latents. It reports distinct refusal-related latents and steering outcomes.
Does not separate harmfulness judgments from refusal decisions.
Does not test cross-language transfer or transfer between base and instruct models for a refusal direction.
Does not manipulate how or when refusal is trained to test whether a single removable direction exists.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2b chat model
rows.operation_detail: Steered input-position activations at layer 13 with the chat decoder vector for latent 70149, scaled by α times its maximum validation activation.
rows.value: The response initially refuses to provide instructions for making cheese, then eventually provides an answer.
rows.note: The authors state that α = 1 is sufficient to influence generation; they also note that the model eventually self-repairs and answers.
rows.check: Single qualitative generation on one harmless prompt, with no rate, no unsteered baseline and no comparison with a refusal direction. It cannot show whether refusal is multi-directional (V4). The steering vector is a crosscoder chat decoder latent, not a difference-in-means direction. Output refuses at first, then answers.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2b chat model
rows.operation_detail: Steered input-position activations at layer 13 with the chat decoder vector for latent 20384, scaled by α times its maximum validation activation.

conditions.value: 20384 (unethical content relating to race, gender and stereotypes)

rows.value: The response initially refuses on grounds concerning harmful stereotypes, then eventually provides an answer.
rows.note: The authors state that α = 5 is needed for optimal effects; the model eventually self-repairs and answers. The refusal rationale differs from that produced by latent 70149.
rows.check: Same as r1: one qualitative example at alpha=5, no rate or baseline. The output is a stereotype disclaimer followed by an answer, so it is arguably not a refusal at all. It does not bear on V4 geometry.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
